feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: Open question on a hypothetical minor “slow-sliding MTP” attack that BIP 54 might introduce
entry.summary: Open Question on a hypothetical minor "slow-sliding MTP" attack introduced by BIP 54 Delving Bitcoin · Nov 21, 2026While reviewing BIP 54, the author raises a hypothetical attack in which the median-time-past (MTP) is gradually pushed away from real-world time, making a block invalid under the timestamp rules. The author notes this would require controlling over 51% of hashrate and would have limited impact. They conclude it does not change their view of BIP 54, but share it as an interesting insight.

entry.title: Node Attestation Protocol: a non-binding way for economic nodes to signal support for Bitcoin proposals
entry.summary: Node Attestation Protocol Delving Bitcoin · Nov 21, 2026This discussion proposes the Node Attestation Protocol (NAP), which lets non-mining economic nodes publish free-form key-value statements backed by cryptographic proof of control of specific UTXOs. An aggregator validates these attestations and sums them by coin value. NAP is explicitly non-binding and intended only as a human-judged signal alongside miner signaling. The post also covers its time and coin-age limits and known weaknesses around privacy and custodial coins.

entry.title: Post Quantum Recovery Framework: a discussion of how unmigrated bitcoin could be recovered if quantum computers break elliptic curve cryptography
entry.summary: Post Quantum Recovery Framework Delving Bitcoin · Nov 21, 2026The author outlines a class of recovery schemes that add extra spending conditions to existing bitcoin UTXOs to protect them from theft if elliptic curve security is broken. It distinguishes prepared schemes, which require user action before that day, from unprepared schemes, and classifies recovery secrets as accidental or essential. The post also describes the dilemma that requiring BIP32 derivation paths could make some coins unspendable, while relying on hidden pubkeys leaves other coins open to theft.

entry.title: Unrig: A prediction market protocol designed to work without liquidity providers and resist manipulation
entry.summary: Unrig: A Prediction Market Protocol That Needs No Liquidity and Can't Be Rigged ethresear.ch · Nov 21, 2026This technical discussion posted on the Ethereum Research forum proposes Unrig, a prediction market protocol built on Ethereum. It claims counterparties form naturally without liquidity provision, and that its mathematical structure makes manipulation unprofitable. The text covers risk pricing, settlement, market creation, outcome determination, and token economics.

entry.title: Isopolia: A Three-Tier Latency Layer-1 Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents
entry.summary: Isopolia: A Three-Tier Latency L1 Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents - Owned-Object FastPay (D4 Fencing), Day-1 X25519 + ML-KEM-768 Privacy, and Endogenous AMM Liquidation Bounds ethresear.ch · Nov 20, 2026This post presents Isopolia, a sovereign Layer-1 protocol and deterministic execution stack built for autonomous AI-agent economies. It covers a three-tier latency design with fast owned-object payments, mutual exclusion between the fast path and BFT consensus, and day-1 hybrid X25519 and ML-KEM-768 privacy for off-chain channels. It also describes endogenous AMM liquidation bounds for compute-lease collateral and Sybil-resistant committee selection.

entry.title: Anatomy of a Fill: how propAMMs trade on Ethereum mainnet
entry.summary: Anatomy of a Fill: PropAMMs on Ethereum ethresear.ch · Nov 20, 2026This post traces one trade through a propAMM on Ethereum, second by second. The market maker streams signed prices to block builders, who write the latest price into the block just before the trade fills. It compares propAMMs with classic AMMs and RFQ designs, and notes that the builders' ordering promise is not enforced by the protocol.

entry.title: Probing Ethereum nodes from outside with Sonar
entry.summary: Probing Ethereum nodes using Sonar ethresear.ch · Nov 19, 2026Sonar is a free beta tool from ProbeLab that tests a single Ethereum node on demand. Given an ENR or other node identifier, it finds the node over discv5, dials each advertised address, and runs the libp2p or devp2p handshake. For consensus-layer nodes it also exchanges Status and MetaData, then compares the results with the node's ENR and past crawl data. The authors ask client teams and node operators what else a probe should check.

entry.title: Encrypted Account: a smart account that keeps its PIN inside the contract
entry.summary: Encrypted Account: a PIN that lives in the contract ethresear.ch · Nov 19, 2026Encrypted Account is an ERC-4337 smart account that stores a PIN inside the contract, encrypted under Zama's threshold FHE, so no server holds the PIN. The contract checks each guess and counts attempts on-chain before the result can be decrypted. It is a research prototype on Sepolia, unaudited and released under the MIT license.

entry.title: Ethereum research forum post: sending an encrypted ePBS payload early and revealing only a key
entry.summary: Reveal a key, not a payload: sending the ePBS payload before the reveal ethresear.ch · Nov 19, 2026This post proposes a change to Gloas (ePBS) in which the builder sends an encrypted payload once a valid block includes its bid, so that the reveal only needs a 32-byte key. The author argues this recovers transfer time lost while the builder waits to reveal. The post also notes that it increases the builder's option to withhold.

entry.title: EIP-8288: Networking Side of Recursive Aggregation
entry.summary: EIP-8288: the networking side of recursive aggregation ethresear.ch · Nov 18, 2026This Ethereum Research forum post studies the networking design of EIP-8288, a bandwidth-efficient mempool based on recursive STARKs. The author used a discrete-event simulator to compare choices such as who aggregates, how raw transactions and proofs travel, when nodes fetch and fold them, and how fast proofs are generated. In a 1,000-node reference network, the results indicate that today's mempool can carry today's load with post-quantum signatures. The post identifies four networking choices that the EIP and the related EIP-8437 should specify.

entry.title: How much bitcoin is held in outputs whose keys or scripts are already public on chain
entry.summary: How much BTC sits behind keys or scripts already on chain (block 975,019) Delving Bitcoin · Nov 18, 2026The author counts unspent outputs at block 975,019 whose public key or script is already visible on chain, finding 7,164,754.12 BTC, or 35.6% of the 20,109,207.36 BTC unspent. The rule applies separately to each output type, and the post adds key reuse counts across P2PK, P2PKH and P2WPKH. Code, extraction rules and result files are published on GitHub.

entry.title: Exploring post-quantum signature aggregation for EIP-8288
entry.summary: Exploring post-quantum signature aggregation for EIP-8288 ethresear.ch · Nov 17, 2026This post explores combining EIP-8141's programmable account validation with EIP-8288's recursive STARK aggregation, so wallets can choose their post-quantum signing scheme while the network verifies one common proof. The author ran five signature schemes (Falcon-512, ML-DSA-44, FORS, Raccoon-128, Raccoon-G) under STARK proofs in leanVM and measured proving, proof-size and verification costs. Because Raccoon-G verification exceeds leanVM's commitment cap, the author splits its matrix computation into five leaf proofs and aggregates them in a Merkle-tree fashion.

entry.title: Garbled STARK verifier for efficient post-quantum Bitcoin bridges
entry.summary: Toward Efficient Post-Quantum Bitcoin Bridges Delving Bitcoin · Nov 16, 2026This Delving Bitcoin discussion presents a garbled-circuit verifier for hash-based STARK proofs, offered as a post-quantum alternative to garbling a Groth16 verifier in BitVM3-style bridges. The authors measure on-chain and off-chain costs using Ethereum mainnet block 26,206,588. The off-chain garbled verifier is about 15 times smaller than BitVM3's Boolean Groth16 verifier, while publishing the proof input on-chain costs over a thousand times BitVM3's Assert.

entry.title: spscand: a Silent Payments scanner for Electrum
entry.summary: Silent Payments for Electrum Delving Bitcoin · Nov 16, 2026The author previously released a Silent Payments sending plugin for Electrum and now introduces spscand, a companion scanner. It finds payments to a user's sp1 address, tracks their spends and reorgs, and reports them through a local JSON API and a webhook. According to the post, it never queries a server about addresses, outputs or transactions, and blocks can come from a user's own node, a blindbit server or BIP352 filters, with Tor supported.

entry.title: Disclosure: Denial-of-service flaw in Core Lightning fixed in v26.06.8
entry.summary: Disclosure: DoS vulnerability fixed in Core Lightning v26.06.8 Delving Bitcoin · Nov 15, 2026A denial-of-service vulnerability in Core Lightning's channel opening flow was fixed in version v26.06.8, and users are advised to upgrade. The flaw (LNF-2026-0004) affected v0.12.0 through v26.06.7, which accepted a funding_created message reusing another channel's funding outpoint, causing two channels to share a channel_id and crashing nodes.

entry.title: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean Delving Bitcoin · Nov 13, 2026The author shares a personal project on Delving Bitcoin that uses STARK proofs to verify parts of Bitcoin consensus. A 1.6 MB proof file is said to verify in a browser in about half a second, covering a header chain from genesis, a replay of blocks 935,001 to 972,500, and the UTXO set after block 972,500, whose hash matches Core's hash_serialized. Scripts and signatures are not covered, and the coin set relies on the same trust as assumeUTXO snapshots.

entry.title: Draft proposal for a post-quantum Bitcoin address format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65 signatures
entry.summary: BIP Draft Post-Quantum Address Format (bc1z) using ML-DSA-65 Delving Bitcoin · Nov 13, 2026This forum post shares a draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal for a new bc1z address format that uses ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) post-quantum signatures. The address commits to a SHA-256 hash of the ML-DSA public key, which is revealed only in the witness at spend time, similar to P2WPKH. The author requests community feedback on address design, parameter choice, soft fork deployment, and migration paths for existing UTXOs.

entry.title: WARCoin: A Proposed 1:1 USD Stablecoin Using Serialized 7-Day Color Buckets and Burn-on-Egress Rules
entry.summary: [RFC] WARCoin: Deterministic 1:1 USD Stablecoin via Serialized 7-Day Color Ring Buffers and Burn-on-Egress Invariants ethresear.ch · Nov 13, 2026This request for comments proposes WARCoin, a deterministic 1:1 USD stablecoin designed to prevent infinite-mint bugs, cross-collateral contagion, and replay attacks. It accepts only USD deposits, burns serial numbers when funds leave, and organizes issuance into seven daily color buckets of 1,000 serials each. A global supply cap of 10^9 serials is enforced, with minting paused when limits are reached.

entry.title: More Meters or More Prices? Comparing One- and Multi-dimensional Ethereum Fee Mechanisms
entry.summary: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum ethresear.ch · Nov 13, 2026This Ethereum Research forum post compares one-dimensional fee mechanisms with the multidimensional fee market proposed in EIP-7999. The author raises the target-to-limit ratio of a normalized benchmark to 4/5 and replaces the EIP-1559 update rule with an EIP-4844-style update, measuring execution gas, state growth, and near-limit blocks. Higher ratios increase execution but push state growth away from its target and raise congestion. The EIP-4844-style update allows lower fees and more execution, but with more congestion.

entry.title: Multi-dimensional decentralization metrics and a double-spend rule open for critique
entry.summary: Multi-dimensional decentralization metrics, and an open question on first-broadcast double-spend rules ethresear.ch · Nov 12, 2026The author presents an open-source Apache-2.0 skill that lets LLM agents analyze blockchain architectures across several independent dimensions rather than a single number, and compares PoW, PoS, DAG, sharded designs and AOB. The post also describes AOB's first-broadcast-wins double-spend rule, which uses an estimated broadcast time t₀ to set waiting periods. The author asks the community to challenge the t₀ error tolerance, adversarial latency model, and eclipse threat model comparison.
